newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl and German miners' leader meet on coal crisis.
newsitem.headline: Kohl and German miners' leader meet on coal crisis.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl and mining union leader Hans Berger began talks on Thursday to try to reach a compromise over a government plan to cut subsidies which has enraged Germany's 90,000 pit workers.
Kohl and Berger met in the chancellery amid reports that Kohl was prepared to offer more government money to cushion the effect of the cuts which miners say will cost 50,000 jobs.
In a sign that quick progress might be made, the government announced a news conference for 10 a.m. (0900 GMT), just an hour after the start of the talks.

As the two sides met, tens of thousands of miners were standing by in nearby Cologne and the Ruhr valley coal-and-steel heartland, ready to resume their protests in Bonn later in the day if the outcome of the talks did not satisfy them.

In a separate protest, thousands of builders were again massing on Berlin's Potsdamer Platz square, Europe's largest construction site, to protest against conditions which they say have put almost a quarter of Germany's 1.7 million builders out of work.

The miners had virtually besieged Bonn's government quarter for three days this week, but withdrew on Wednesday after Kohl postponed talks planned for Tuesday at short notice, saying he would not negotiate in a climate of intimidation.
On Thursday morning commuter traffic was flowing normally through the city's main drive for the first time since Friday.

Police maintained a strong presence and kept crowd barriers at the ready. But only a handful of miners were left as a reminder of the thousands who unnerved the city earlier in the week with protests which briefly spilled over into violence.
The mountains of bottles, drinks cans, disposable plates and cigarette butts they left behind had largely been cleared away.
Bonn plans to cut the level of annual subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) by 2005 from more than nine billion marks at present.

The mass-circulation daily newspaper Bild said Kohl was ready to offer an extra 300 million marks a year for the next three years to delay some pit closures, as long as the Social Democrat-led government of the coal mining state of North Rhine-Westphalia increased its own subsidies over the next eight years.
Kohl had said on Wednesday he saw chances of an agreement, and coalition sources said they were considering improving welfare benefits for miners to ease the pain of the cuts.

But the pressure remained on from 8,000 brawny pit workers from Saar state on the French border, who had held a raucous rally in Bonn on Wednesday, and who spent the night in a tented village in the grounds of Cologne football stadium.
"If we don't get a reasonable result, we'll be back and all hell will be let loose," one miner from Saarbruecken had said on Wednesday.
Kohl had said he believed the talks would succeed "with a bit of goodwill". But he insisted his plan was fair.

Miners in Germany's 18 pits walked out last Friday after Bonn announced the cuts, arguing that it could no longer afford to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is more than three times the world market price.
IG Bergbau says the plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.

Some commentators have cautioned Kohl against backing down too far and laying his government open to pressure from all sides to give up the strict budget discipline necessary to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The danger of an increasingly aggressive wave of demonstrations is completely real," the daily newspaper Die Welt said. ($ = 1.695 German Marks)
